question_text: A RAG pipeline answers questions from technical API documentation with headings, sections, and nested subsections. Which chunking strategy best preserves contextual coherence?

options.text: Fixed-size chunking at 512 tokens with 10% overlap
Hierarchical chunking that splits on heading and section boundaries
Sentence-level chunking where each sentence is one chunk
No chunking — load each document as a single embedding

explanation: Skill 1.5.1 describes hierarchical chunking based on content structure as optimal for structured documents. Splitting at heading boundaries keeps related information together within each chunk. Fixed-size chunking may break mid-section. Sentence-level chunking loses paragraph context. Whole-document embeddings exceed most embedding model token limits and lose retrieval granularity.
source_topic: Chunking strategies, Bedrock Knowledge Bases chunking

question_text: A company is choosing an embedding model for a multilingual medical literature RAG system. Which THREE factors should guide their selection?

options.text: Embedding dimensionality — must match the vector store's configured index dimension
Domain performance — benchmarks on biomedical text
The model's parameter count
Multilingual support — handles all languages in the corpus
The visual design of the model card documentation

explanation: Skill 1.5.2 cites evaluating Amazon Titan embeddings based on dimensionality and domain fit, and evaluating performance characteristics of Bedrock embedding models. (A) Dimensions must match the configured vector store index. (B) Biomedical domain fit directly determines retrieval quality. (D) Multilingual support is essential for a multilingual corpus. Parameter count alone does not predict embedding quality. Documentation aesthetics are irrelevant.
source_topic: Amazon Titan Embeddings, embedding model selection

question_text: A legal research tool must find both exact statutory citations (e.g., '42 U.S.C. § 1983') and conceptually related cases. Which retrieval approach handles both requirements?

options.text: Pure dense vector cosine similarity search
Pure BM25 keyword search
Hybrid search — combine BM25 keyword scoring with dense vector similarity using reciprocal rank fusion
Amazon Neptune graph traversal for legal citation chains

explanation: Skill 1.5.4 explicitly names 'hybrid search that combines keywords and vectors.' BM25 handles exact citation matching where semantic search fails; dense vector search finds conceptually related cases. Pure vector search misses exact matches. Pure BM25 misses semantic relevance. Neptune graph traversal suits citation-graph navigation but doesn't provide a general keyword+semantic search capability.
source_topic: Hybrid search, BM25, OpenSearch

question_text: A RAG system retrieves 20 candidate chunks for broad recall, but only 5 can be passed to the FM due to context window constraints. How should the top-5 be selected?

options.text: Randomly sample 5 from the 20 retrieved chunks
Always take the top-5 by initial cosine similarity score
Apply an Amazon Bedrock reranker model that scores each of the 20 candidates against the query and selects the top-5
Use Amazon Textract to re-parse the source documents and pick the first 5 pages

explanation: Skill 1.5.4 explicitly cites Amazon Bedrock reranker models as part of advanced search architectures. A cross-encoder reranker scores each (query, chunk) pair with much higher accuracy than cosine similarity alone — the standard RAG reranking pattern. Random sampling loses quality. Initial cosine scores are good for recall but cross-encoder reranking improves precision. Textract re-parsing bypasses the retrieval system entirely.
source_topic: Amazon Bedrock reranker, RAG reranking

question_text: Users query a RAG system with very short, ambiguous questions like 'fix login error'. Retrieval quality is poor. How can this be improved without retraining the embedding model?

options.text: Increase top-k retrieval count to 100 to cover all possible matches
Use Amazon Bedrock to generate multiple semantically rich query variants from the original, then union or merge their retrieval results
Reduce chunk size so individual chunks are more specific
Switch to a larger generation FM to compensate for poor retrieval

explanation: Skill 1.5.5 describes query expansion via Amazon Bedrock — rewriting a short query into richer variants that capture different aspects of intent, then merging retrieved results. Increasing top-k (A) reduces precision and bloats context. Reducing chunk size (C) may hurt recall for broad queries. Switching generation FMs (D) doesn't fix a retrieval problem.
source_topic: Query expansion, Amazon Bedrock, RAG

question_text: A user asks: 'Compare the refund policies of our Premium and Standard plans.' This requires retrieving information from two separate policy sections. Which retrieval strategy handles this best?

options.text: Submit the compound question directly to the vector store
Use Lambda to decompose the query into sub-queries ('Premium plan refund' and 'Standard plan refund'), retrieve each separately, then merge before generation
Increase top-k to 50 and hope both topics appear in the results
Ask the user to rephrase the question as two separate queries

explanation: Skill 1.5.5 describes Lambda functions for query decomposition as a sophisticated query handling approach. Atomic sub-queries each retrieve dedicated evidence for their sub-topic; merging the results ensures both topics are covered before the FM generates a comparison. Submitting the compound query biases retrieval toward whichever sub-topic has stronger vector representation. High top-k inflates context without improving precision. User-side reformulation degrades UX.
source_topic: Query decomposition, Lambda, RAG

question_text: A team needs to generate embeddings for 10 million document chunks stored in S3 within a 4-hour window. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Call the Bedrock embedding API sequentially from a single Lambda function
Use SQS to fan out batch embedding requests to multiple Lambda workers calling Amazon Bedrock in parallel
Download all documents to a single EC2 instance and run a local embedding model
Use Amazon Polly to convert documents to audio, then create audio embeddings

explanation: Skill 1.5.2 cites Lambda functions for batch embedding generation. An SQS + Lambda fan-out pattern parallelises across thousands of concurrent invocations, processing 10M chunks within the time window while respecting Bedrock API quota controls. Sequential single-Lambda calls would take far too long. A single EC2 instance has limited CPU/GPU throughput. Amazon Polly produces speech audio — irrelevant for text embeddings.
source_topic: Batch embedding, SQS, Lambda, Bedrock embeddings

question_text: A team builds multiple AI agents using different frameworks. They want all agents to access the same vector search capability through a standardised, framework-agnostic protocol. What achieves this?

options.text: Write a custom HTTP client library for each agent framework
Implement an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server for vector search; agents use MCP clients to call it via the standard protocol
Embed the vector search logic inside each FM's system prompt
Create separate API Gateway endpoints for each agent framework

explanation: Skill 1.5.6 explicitly mentions Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients for vector queries and standardised API patterns for retrieval augmentation. MCP provides a vendor-neutral protocol enabling any MCP-compatible agent to call the same vector search resource. Per-framework HTTP clients defeat standardisation. System prompts cannot execute code. Separate API Gateway endpoints per framework creates fragmented governance rather than a standard protocol.
source_topic: Model Context Protocol (MCP), RAG, agent tool access

question_text: A global enterprise stores HR policy documents in English, French, and German. Employees query the knowledge base in their native language. Retrieval quality is poor when the query language differs from the document language. Which solution addresses this?

options.text: Replace the monolingual English embeddings model with a multilingual embeddings model that maps semantically equivalent text across languages to nearby vectors
Translate all documents to English and delete the originals before indexing
Create a separate knowledge base for each language with no cross-base retrieval
Use keyword search only, which is language-agnostic by nature

explanation: A multilingual embeddings model places semantically similar text from different languages close together in the shared vector space, enabling a French query to match German or English documents correctly. Translating and discarding originals loses fidelity and legal retention obligations. Separate per-language bases require the user to know which language the answer is in. Keyword search is not language-agnostic — it only matches exact tokens, missing cross-lingual synonyms.
source_topic: Multilingual embeddings, cross-lingual semantic search

question_text: A RAG system retrieves very specific sentence fragments that lack surrounding context, causing the FM to generate incomplete answers. Which chunking strategy BEST resolves this issue?

options.text: Increase fixed chunk size to 5,000 tokens
Use hierarchical chunking: embed small child chunks for precise search, return larger parent chunks at retrieval time
Reduce chunk overlap to zero to avoid redundancy
Use only keyword-based BM25 search instead of vector search

explanation: Hierarchical chunking solves the precision vs. context trade-off: small child chunks enable precise vector matching, but the retrieved context returned to the FM is the larger parent chunk, providing the surrounding context needed for complete answers. Simply increasing chunk size reduces precision. Eliminating overlap worsens boundary issues. Switching to pure keyword search doesn't address the context problem.
source_topic: Hierarchical chunking for context-rich retrieval

question_text: A developer is chunking legal contracts for a RAG system. The contracts have well-defined sections and subsections with headings. Which chunking strategy will BEST preserve the meaning of each section?

options.text: Fixed-size chunking at 300 characters with no overlap
Semantic/recursive chunking that splits at natural section boundaries (headings and paragraphs)
Random splitting of the document into equal-length segments
Character-level tokenisation and storage of individual sentences

explanation: Legal contracts have clear structural boundaries (sections, clauses, articles). Semantic/recursive chunking that respects these natural boundaries ensures each chunk represents a complete, meaningful unit (e.g., a full clause). Fixed-size chunking at 300 characters would frequently cut mid-sentence or mid-clause. Random splitting is semantically meaningless. Individual sentence storage loses clause-level context.
source_topic: Semantic chunking for structured documents

question_text: A RAG system retrieves the top 20 chunks from OpenSearch using vector similarity. However, the most relevant chunks are often ranked 10-15 in the results, and only the top 5 are sent to the FM. What is the BEST way to improve the quality of the final top-5 context?

options.text: Increase the number of chunks sent to the FM from 5 to 20
Apply a Bedrock reranker model to re-score and reorder the 20 retrieved chunks before selecting the top 5
Use a smaller embedding model with lower dimensionality
Reduce the chunk size to improve initial vector similarity scores

explanation: Reranking uses a more powerful cross-encoder model to re-score all retrieved candidates in the context of the actual query, significantly improving the relevance ordering compared to embedding-based similarity alone. Sending all 20 chunks to the FM inflates token cost and may reduce answer quality due to noise. A smaller embedding model would likely worsen retrieval. Smaller chunks don't directly address the reranking problem.
source_topic: Bedrock reranker for RAG relevance improvement

question_text: A RAG system performs well on broad, conceptual queries but misses exact product codes like 'SKU-99214-B'. Users complain that searching for specific codes returns irrelevant results. What retrieval enhancement BEST addresses this?

options.text: Switch to a larger, more capable embedding model
Enable hybrid search combining keyword (BM25) search with vector similarity search
Increase chunk overlap to 50%
Add more training examples to the fine-tuned model

explanation: Exact identifiers (SKU codes, model numbers, specific terms) are best matched by keyword/lexical search (BM25), which performs exact and near-exact matching. Pure vector search captures semantics but may not match specific identifiers precisely. Hybrid search combines both approaches — keyword for exact matches, vectors for semantic matches — and merges/re-ranks the results. A larger embedding model still may not match arbitrary codes exactly. Chunk overlap and fine-tuning don't address the retrieval methodology.
source_topic: Hybrid search for exact + semantic retrieval

question_text: Users search for 'ML platform' but the knowledge base contains documents using 'machine learning infrastructure'. The search returns poor results because the terms don't overlap semantically in the embedding space. What query processing technique addresses this?

options.text: Query compression — shorten the query before searching
Query expansion — use a Bedrock call to generate synonyms and related terms, then search for all of them
Query decomposition — split the query into sub-queries
Increase the vector store's k (number of results) from 5 to 50

explanation: Query expansion augments the original query with synonyms and related terms (generated by an FM) to improve recall. Searching for 'ML platform OR machine learning infrastructure OR MLOps platform' captures documents that the original query would miss. Query compression reduces token count but doesn't improve retrieval. Query decomposition handles multi-part questions. Increasing k returns more results but many may be irrelevant, increasing noise sent to the FM.
source_topic: Query expansion for improved RAG recall

question_text: A user asks a RAG assistant: 'Compare the return policies and warranty terms of Product A and Product B.' The knowledge base stores these as separate documents. A single vector search returns mixed results. What query processing strategy BEST handles this?

options.text: Increase the number of retrieved chunks (k) to include both topics
Decompose the query into two sub-queries ('return policy for Product A' and 'warranty terms for Product B'), retrieve separately, then synthesise
Use semantic chunking to combine Product A and B information into single chunks
Switch to a multimodal embedding model

explanation: Query decomposition breaks a complex comparative question into focused sub-queries, each targeting a specific retrieval task. This yields precise, relevant chunks for each sub-topic, which are then synthesised by the FM into a coherent comparison. Simply increasing k mixes both topics chaotically. Combining products in the same chunks would destroy retrieval precision. A multimodal model doesn't address multi-topic retrieval.
source_topic: Query decomposition for complex multi-topic queries

topic: Bedrock Knowledge Base RetrieveAndGenerate vs Retrieve API
question_text: A developer wants to evaluate the retrieval quality of a Bedrock Knowledge Base independently of the generation quality. They want to see exactly which chunks are retrieved for a given query before the FM generates a response. Which Bedrock API should they use?

options.text: RetrieveAndGenerate
InvokeModel
Retrieve
StartBatchInferenceJob

explanation: The Bedrock Retrieve API performs retrieval-only from a Knowledge Base, returning the chunks and their relevance scores without invoking a generative model. This enables independent evaluation of retrieval quality (are the right documents being found?). RetrieveAndGenerate combines retrieval + generation in one call, making it impossible to isolate the retrieval step. InvokeModel calls a model directly without a knowledge base. StartBatchInferenceJob is for large-scale async inference.
source_topic: Bedrock Retrieve API for retrieval-only evaluation

topic: Embedding model version drift — RAG silent failure
question_text: A RAG system that was working well suddenly starts returning poor-quality answers after a pipeline update. The vector index was not re-built. Investigation shows the embedding model version was updated in the ingestion pipeline but not in the query pipeline. What type of failure is this?

options.text: Context window overflow
Embedding model version mismatch causing semantic drift between index vectors and query vectors
Guardrail false positive blocking valid retrievals
FM hallucination due to poor prompt engineering

explanation: Embedding vectors are only comparable if generated by the same model version. If the ingestion pipeline uses model v1 (stored in the index) but the query pipeline now uses model v2, the query vectors exist in a different semantic space than the index vectors — similarity scores become meaningless and retrieval quality collapses silently. This is a common production failure that requires rebuilding the index with the new model. The other options describe different failure modes.
source_topic: Embedding model version mismatch in RAG

topic: Bedrock Knowledge Base RetrieveAndGenerate vs Retrieve API
question_text: A developer wants to build a chatbot that automatically retrieves relevant context from a knowledge base and generates a grounded response in a single API call, without writing custom retrieval-generation orchestration code. Which Bedrock API is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Retrieve
RetrieveAndGenerate
InvokeModel with a knowledge base ARN parameter
StartBatchInferenceJob

explanation: RetrieveAndGenerate is the managed, single-call Bedrock API that performs both retrieval from a Knowledge Base and generation using an FM — grounding responses in documents to reduce hallucinations, with no custom orchestration required. The Retrieve API is retrieval-only. InvokeModel has no built-in knowledge base retrieval parameter. StartBatchInferenceJob is for async large-scale processing, not real-time chat.
source_topic: RetrieveAndGenerate for managed RAG in single call

question_text: A developer is configuring Bedrock Knowledge Base chunking for a collection of technical FAQs. Each FAQ has a clear question-and-answer pair that fits in about 200 tokens. They want to avoid FAQ answers being split across chunks. Which chunking strategy is BEST?

options.text: Fixed-size chunking at 100 tokens with no overlap
Semantic chunking that splits at natural section boundaries (each Q&A pair as one chunk)
Fixed-size chunking at 5,000 tokens to ensure everything fits
Random chunking optimised for embedding model performance

explanation: For structured FAQ content where each Q&A is a natural semantic unit, semantic chunking that respects section boundaries ensures each chunk is a complete, self-contained FAQ entry. This maximises retrieval relevance (a full Q&A is retrieved, not half a question or half an answer). 100-token fixed chunking would split answers. 5,000-token chunks would merge many FAQs together. There is no 'random chunking' optimisation.
source_topic: Semantic chunking for structured FAQ content

question_text: A team needs to generate embeddings for 500,000 document chunks stored in S3. They want to optimise for cost and throughput rather than real-time latency. Which approach is MOST cost-efficient?

options.text: Call InvokeModel in a Lambda for each chunk individually in parallel
Use Bedrock Batch Inference (StartBatchInferenceJob) to process all chunks asynchronously from S3
Use Bedrock Provisioned Throughput with synchronous InvokeModel calls
Host the embedding model on SageMaker real-time endpoints with auto-scaling

explanation: Bedrock Batch Inference is optimised for large-scale asynchronous processing: you submit all 500K chunks via S3, and Bedrock processes them in bulk at lower effective cost per token. Individual Lambda-per-chunk invocations incur per-request overhead and concurrency management complexity. Provisioned Throughput is for steady real-time traffic, not batch. SageMaker endpoints require custom containers and infrastructure management.
source_topic: Bedrock Batch Inference for bulk embedding generation

question_text: Before submitting a large prompt to Amazon Bedrock, a developer wants to estimate the cost by counting how many tokens the prompt contains — without actually running inference. Which Bedrock API enables this?

options.text: GetFoundationModel
InvokeModel with max_tokens set to 0
CountTokens
ListFoundationModels

explanation: The Bedrock CountTokens API returns the token count for a given input without running inference — useful for cost estimation, prompt budget management, and avoiding context window overflows before making actual inference calls. GetFoundationModel and ListFoundationModels return metadata about models. InvokeModel with max_tokens=0 would still trigger an inference attempt and incur input token costs.
source_topic: CountTokens API for cost estimation without inference

question_text: A RAG application answers complex, abstract questions where the user's short query rarely shares vocabulary with the relevant source passages, so pure semantic search over the raw query returns poor matches. Which retrieval technique is specifically designed to close this query-document vocabulary gap?

options.text: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) — have the LLM generate a hypothetical answer, embed that, and search with its vector
Increase the top-K value so more chunks are returned
Switch the vector index from HNSW to IVF
Lower the embedding model's dimension count to reduce noise

explanation: HyDE asks the LLM to write a hypothetical document that would answer the question, then embeds THAT richer text instead of the sparse query. The hypothetical answer shares far more vocabulary and semantic structure with real source passages, dramatically improving retrieval for abstract questions. Raising top-K only returns more low-relevance chunks; the HNSW/IVF choice is an ANN algorithm tradeoff unrelated to the vocabulary gap; reducing dimensions degrades embedding quality.
source_topic: HyDE hypothetical document embeddings for retrieval

question_text: Users ask highly specific questions (e.g. "What was the tax treatment of the 2023 R&D credit for a Delaware C-corp with under $5M revenue?") but the knowledge base stores broad conceptual documents. Retrieval on the narrow query misses the relevant conceptual passages. Which retrieval strategy best addresses this?

options.text: Step-back prompting — generate a broader, more general query to retrieve high-level context before answering the specific question
Reduce chunk size so each chunk is more specific
Disable hybrid search and use keyword-only matching
Increase temperature on the generation model

explanation: Step-back prompting has the LLM first derive a broader/more abstract version of the question, retrieves the general conceptual context that specific queries miss, then answers the narrow question grounded in that context. Smaller chunks make the specificity mismatch worse; keyword-only search would still miss conceptual overlap; temperature affects generation randomness, not retrieval.
source_topic: Step-back prompting to retrieve broader context

question_text: A knowledge base stores chunks with rich metadata (department, created_date, access_level). Users ask questions like "Show me engineering docs updated after January 2026." Pure vector similarity ignores these structured constraints and returns stale or wrong-department results. Which retrieval approach fixes this most directly?

options.text: Self-querying retrieval — the LLM parses the natural-language query into a semantic search string PLUS structured metadata filters that are applied during retrieval
Re-embed all documents with a larger embedding model
Store every document in a single flat index with no metadata
Always retrieve the top 100 chunks and let the LLM sort them out

explanation: Self-querying uses the LLM to translate the user's question into both a semantic query and explicit metadata filters (e.g. department = engineering AND last_updated > 2026-01-01), so the vector store applies precise structured constraints alongside similarity. A bigger embedding model does not enforce date/department constraints; removing metadata eliminates the very signal needed; dumping 100 chunks on the LLM is costly and still returns wrong-department noise.
source_topic: Self-querying retrieval generating metadata filters
